newsitem.title: USA: Fundraising scandal raises yawns outside capital.
newsitem.headline: Fundraising scandal raises yawns outside capital.

text.p: Inside the U.S. capital, a growing campaign fund-raising scandal has become a media feeding frenzy. In the rest of America, it's a big yawn.

President Bill Clinton cannot appear before the media without being bombarded with questions on the latest developments. His spokesman, Mike McCurry, said the President "is well aware we are in the middle of a feeding frenzy and you just have to endure it."

After weeks of revelations about the way Clinton and Vice President Al Gore used the White House to raise money for the Democratic Party, about mysterious contributions from shadowy Asian interests and most recently about alleged covert attempts by China to influence U.S. politicians, most Americans remain indifferent.
"This is not getting much play outside of Washington," said Gary Jacobson, a politician scientist with the University of California, San Diego.

"As long as there are no visible signs that policy was either made or changed because of some quid pro quo, this so-called scandal will remain at the level of fuzziness. It's hard to show what is illegal here," he said.

Polls show widespread public cynicism about the fund-raising practices of both political parties. Democrat Clinton's approval ratings have slipped a bit but still remain remarkably strong. In a CBS poll this week, only 16 percent of respondents said they were following the story very closely.

According to a Harris poll, two thirds of voters believe there is no difference between the parties in how much they are influenced by campaign contributors and 76 percent thought Congress was "largely owned by special interest groups."

Political historian Allan Lichtman of American University in Washington said the Republican failure to make the scandal resound with the public was partly because of their ceaseless attacks on Clinton's morals over the past five years.
"The Republicans have attacked Clinton on ethics for so long without pinning anything on him, they are now in the position of a party that cried wolf," Lichtman said.
In recent days, after months of focusing on the White House and the Democrats, the media has begun to uncover some Republican practices that look a little seamy.

A Senate decision Tuesday to widen its probe to include improper as well as illegal campaign fund raising is likely to increase public cynicism still further, while making it more difficult for voters to distinguish between practices that may be unseemly and those that are actually against the law.
For Georgetown University scholar Steven Wayne, public indifference can be traced to a healthy economy and a general sense of well-being in the land.
"If the economy stays strong and inflation is low and the stock market keeps going up and crime goes down, this story may continue to be a big yawn," he said.
"If the economy starts going bad, Clinton will drop like a stone and all this will come to the fore."

Still, the affair has already affected the political process. It has tarnished Gore's previously spotless reputation and may encourage other Democrats to challenge him for the party's presidential nomination in 2000.
More immediately, the scandal has reduced Clinton's ability to set an agenda and may weaken him in budget negotiations with the Republicans, which are already moving painfully slowly.
With the Republicans in Congress apparently drifting without effective leadership, there is a sense of paralysis in the capital.
"We have leaderless government at the moment, but that doesn't matter as long as times are good," said Wayne.
